content.text: In a **deductive** argument, true premises guarantee the conclusion. In an **inductive** argument, true premises only make it probable.

content.definition: Most A are B. This is an A. So this is probably a B.

examples.title: A strong one
lines: 90% of students who study every week pass the exam.
examples.note: Strong, but not valid: Maria could be among the 10% who fail.

examples.title: A weak one
lines: 55% of voters in this town favor the plan.
examples.conclusion: So Lee probably favors the plan.
examples.note: The premises give only weak support. Inductive strength comes in degrees.

options: Its conclusion could be false even if every premise is true
It has more than two premises
question.hint: Compare it with a valid deductive argument. What cannot happen there?
question.explanation: In an inductive argument, true premises make the conclusion probable, not certain. The conclusion can still be false.
